claims.text: Coupled degradation under tribo-corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by a tribo-chemical feedback loop.
Mechanical sliding intermittently removes the protective passive oxide film.
Removal of the passive film exposes fresh, high-energy alloy surfaces that are more vulnerable to corrosion.
Corrosion of the exposed surface produces localized pits.
Corrosion-induced pitting weakens the local microstructure.
Pitting and corrosion-induced weakening accelerate subsequent mechanical wear.
The feedback between wear and corrosion causes total tribo-corrosion degradation to exceed the sum of isolated wear and corrosion degradation.
The initial alloy has a robust passive oxide film that provides corrosion resistance under static conditions.
Boron microalloying can enhance passive-film stability in a high-entropy alloy.
Boron microalloying can promote faster passive-film reformation.
The integrity and reformation kinetics of the passive film mediate the coupled response.
Localized-pit formation and propagation mediate the coupled response.
A compositionally modified alloy can serve as a matched comparison that isolates passive-film integrity as the governing cause.
Enhancing oxide-film stability will reduce the alloy's individual corrosion rate.
Enhancing oxide-film stability will reduce the alloy's individual wear rate.
Enhancing oxide-film stability will reduce the synergistic component of tribo-corrosion degradation.
The predicted feedback should operate when passive-film reformation is slower than film removal by wear.
The predicted feedback may fail when the passive film reforms rapidly enough to counterbalance mechanical removal.
Tribo-corrosion effect sizes and the relative wear and corrosion contributions depend on load, sliding speed, corrosive-medium concentration, and alloy composition.
Failure to observe either super-additive degradation or a reduction of synergy after enhancing film stability would falsify the proposed feedback loop.
